question:
For every positive integer d, work on C^d tensor C^d and let Phi=|Phi_d><Phi_d|, where |Phi_d>=(1/sqrt(d))*sum_{i=1}^d |i,i>. Thus Phi is a rank-one trace-one projector. Put rho_d(x)=(1-x)*Phi+(x/d^2)*I for any real x, without a sign restriction.

Assess the predecessor's dimension-independent assertion that rho_d(x) is a density operator exactly for x in[0,d^2/(d^2-1)], with two tight finite endpoints. Is that assertion valid at every allowed d? Determine the exact set of real x for each dimension branch, treating d=1 explicitly rather than inserting d>=2 as a standing premise.

Prove trace1 holds for all real x. For d>=2, diagonalize rho_d(x) on the range of Phi and its orthogonal complement, give eigenvalues and multiplicities, derive the exact full positivity interval and exhibit a negative-expectation unit vector on each side outside it. Identify the endpoint states/ranks. For d=1, compute the whole family directly, explain why a coefficient on a zero-rank complementary projector imposes no positivity constraint, and say why there are no two finite boundary endpoints in this case. Explain why d=0 does not support the stipulated trace-one Phi, without dividing by zero. This is only a density-positivity calculation, not an entanglement or PPT classification.
reference_answer:
The predecessor's universal finite-interval assertion is false/inapplicable at d=1: the denominator d^2-1 then vanishes and the proposed lower constraint x>=0 is false. At d=1, Phi=I=1 on the one-dimensional joint space, so rho_1(x)=(1-x)+x=1 for EVERY real x. In particular x=-1 is still a positive trace-one state. The exact allowed set in this branch is R, not a finite interval with two tight endpoints. The label x is redundant there.

For any positive d, tr(Phi)=1 and tr(I)=d^2 give tr(rho_d(x))=1-x+(x/d^2)d^2=1 for every real x. The operator is Hermitian for real x. Write rho_d(x)=a Phi+b(I-Phi), with a=1-x+x/d^2 and b=x/d^2. These are coefficients of two orthogonal projectors, not necessarily two different numerical eigenvalues: at x=1 they coincide. For d>=2 both subspaces are nonzero, with ranks1 and d^2-1 respectively. Thus the spectrum is a with multiplicity1 and b with multiplicity d^2-1, and positivity is equivalent to a>=0 and b>=0.

Since d^2>0, b>=0 iff x>=0. Also 1-1/d^2>0 when d>=2, so a=1-x(1-1/d^2)>=0 iff x<=L_d=d^2/(d^2-1). Hence the exact allowed interval is[0,L_d]. If x<0, the unit product vector |1,2>, available for every d>=2, is orthogonal to |Phi_d> and has expectation b<0. If x>L_d, the unit vector |Phi_d> has expectation a<0. These witnesses prove necessity and sharpness, while nonnegative a,b prove sufficiency. At x=0 the state is Phi of rank1; at x=L_d it is (I-Phi)/(d^2-1), of rank d^2-1. At either endpoint the named eigenvalue is zero and becomes negative immediately outside. There is no condition x<=1: x can exceed1 up to L_d while both spectral coefficients remain nonnegative.

At d=1 the same algebraic coefficients reduce to a=1,b=x, but I-Phi=0 has rank0. Thus b is NOT an actual eigenvalue of any nonzero spectral sector, and requiring b>=0 is invalid. The sole actual eigenvalue is1, independent of x; there is no division by d^2-1 or a vanishing-eigenvalue endpoint argument. At d=0 there cannot be a rank-one trace-one projector at all: the zero-dimensional space has only the zero operator with trace0, so the premise of this family is unsatisfied. One must not define |Phi_d> or x/d^2 at d=0.

This proves the complete dimension-branch positivity statement without hiding a d>=2 standing assumption. The source Exercise6.2/Prop6.8 gives the nontrivial isotropic interval, but its parameter expression does not define the one-dimensional boundary by itself. This is an explicit change to the requested question; the historical claim is preserved for assessment, not silently accepted. No separability, partial-transpose criterion, quantum implementation or new local formal proof is inferred from positivity alone.
